The essentials

Getting started

Find the right tone. Shape the contrast. Give the highlights room to shine.

A practical guide to developing photos in Dark Melon, from a simple first edit to a consistent film-inspired collection.

Make your first edit ↓

01 / Start here

A good edit can be simple.

Choose Open Image… to load a photo, or select one in the folder browser. Start with a RAW file if you have one. Dark Melon also opens ordinary SDR and HDR images.

  1. Set Tone around your subject.

    Move Tone until the gray overlay falls on the brightness you want to preserve. For a portrait, try the transition between the lit and shaded parts of the skin. For other scenes, choose an important midtone.

  2. Adjust Contrast.

    Find a pleasing balance around that tone. Start at zero or above; negative values are available for deliberate low-contrast looks.

  3. Check the highlights in HDR.

    Press H to compare HDR and SDR. Read HDR Output above the histogram. Around 4–8× SDR white is a useful starting point for this workflow, not a required target. Use HDR Rolloff to shape the highlight brightness.

  4. Export a photo; save the edit if you want to keep it.

    Export creates an image to share. Save keeps the development settings beside the original, so you can return to the edit. These are separate actions.

In this example, the SDR curve rolls toward white while HDR preserves more highlight separation, reaching 4.49× SDR white. The goal is to retain natural shadows and midtones while allowing bright parts of the scene to look brighter.

Already happy with the result? You can stop here. The remaining sections explain the controls for when you need them.

02 / Find your way

The toolbar & HDR preview

From left to right: Export, Save development settings, Lock Film, the working color space, and HDR preview.

HDR button · H
Switches the preview between HDR and SDR. Preview selection and export format are separate: choose the HDR mode you want in the export options.
sRGB · Display P3 · Rec.2020
Choose the working color space. These spaces have different color boundaries, which you can see in the color scopes. Rec.2020 is useful for the log-LUT workflow described below.
Original · hold C
Temporarily compares against the default SDR development while retaining your transform. Release the key or button to return to the edit.

To judge HDR highlights, use an HDR-capable display with HDR enabled where required. The available brightness depends on the display and system settings. A conventional SDR display cannot show the full HDR result; the output number is a brightness ratio, not a guarantee of what your screen can reproduce.

03 / Brightness with intent

Tone, Contrast & ISO

Tone identifies the luminance region around which you want to shape the image. Contrast changes the tonal separation around it, generally preserving the chosen tone’s brightness. Set Tone first, then judge Contrast.

HDR Gain
Multiplies the entire HDR curve. 1× keeps the automatically calculated rendition; 2× doubles its linear brightness. Zero turns HDR off.
HDR Rolloff
Changes how the HDR curve bends through the highlights. Zero gives a straight extension; positive values flatten its upper end. Watch the curve and HDR Output as you adjust.
White point
Sets the source level mapped to SDR white. Moving it independently of Tone gives you more control over the shape of the SDR curve.

Want a familiar exposure control?

Use ISO. It moves the SDR white point and Tone together, providing an exposure-like adjustment while preserving their relationship.

The displayed value is an effective ISO: capture ISO adjusted for the digital exposure changes. It does not change how the original photo was captured or recover clipped detail. Camera ISO can also affect noise, gain, and highlight headroom, so a post-processing adjustment is not universally identical to changing ISO in-camera.

04 / Color

White balance & saturation

Dark Melon has two white-balance stages: RAW temperature/tint in the decoder and RGB white balance later in the pipeline. Either can help with a normal digital edit; their different positions matter more when building a film look.

Drag in the vectorscope to shift the photo’s tint. To neutralize an area, activate the white-balance picker with W, click a center in the preview, drag out a circle, then click again to apply. Choose an area that should be neutral, with enough pixels to average out noise.

Chroma → Chroma

This graph adjusts color intensity according to how colorful a pixel already is. 1× leaves chroma unchanged. Increase the multipliers for stronger color, or reduce them for a quieter palette.

For a saturation-like change, adjust the multipliers across the range together. For a vibrance-like change, move SDR ½ while leaving the stronger colors nearer their existing level. These are useful analogies, not exact matches to another app’s saturation or vibrance algorithm.

The Mountain Range

Colors run horizontally; chroma, or color intensity, runs vertically. The boundary near the top shows the maximum chroma for each hue in the selected working space and rendition. A color at the SDR boundary may still fit within HDR’s larger available range. Switch HDR preview to see the corresponding boundary.

Use the color handles to adjust individual hues and their chroma. Judge the image as well as the scope: the boundary describes the available range, not a target that every color should reach.

05 / Start with the source

RAW controls

Dark Melon uses Apple’s RAW decoder. The available controls and decoder options depend on the file and system.

RAW9
Uses Apple’s neural demosaic and denoise when available. It can change detail, texture, and color, and may take longer to process. Compare the result at a useful zoom level and choose the rendition you prefer.
Exposure & Max Range
RAW Exposure changes the signal before the main tone controls. In this workflow, use it primarily to fit useful highlight information into the working range. Max Range does this automatically. You can enable Always maximize RAW range in Settings for RAW files without saved or pending edits.
Shadow Bias
Crops the darkest part of the signal for deeper blacks. Use 0 when preserving extreme shadow detail is important.
Offset
Adds the same offset to linear RGB. Positive values lift black; negative values clip shadows. Small adjustments can help with files whose useful detail is buried near black.

Keep useful highlight information when possible: those relative brightness values give the HDR rendition room to preserve the scene’s bright areas. Use the main Tone and ISO controls for the overall appearance.

06 / A different rendering

Film looks with LUTs

A LUT transforms colors according to a predefined look. Its expected input and output matter: a log LUT needs a different signal from a LUT designed for sRGB.

Using a log LUT

  1. In Library, choose Add → Add LUT… and import a .cube file.
  2. Right-click the LUT and choose Configure LUT…. Match both its input and output gamma/gamut to the LUT’s documentation.
  3. Choose Rec.2020 as the working color space. Enable HDR Gain. For the example workflow, start with Contrast 0, HDR Rolloff 0, and HDR Gain 5.0, then inspect the straight HDR curve. This is a starting point, not a universal LUT calibration.
  4. Select the LUT and adjust HDR Gain to set the brightness entering the look. You can also adjust Tone and Contrast before the LUT to shape its result.

HDR in, SDR out. Log-input LUTs use the processed HDR image as their input and currently produce an SDR rendition. The pre-LUT SDR appearance is not the input to the look. With HDR Gain off, the log LUT is bypassed.

Using an sRGB LUT

Set both profiles to sRGB for a LUT designed for sRGB input and output. These LUTs retain HDR output, but the app grades the SDR rendition and reconstructs HDR using the original HDR-to-SDR relationship. It does not directly send extended HDR values through the LUT. Check bright colors and transitions in both previews, especially with strong looks.

07 / Keep your work

Save, export & snapshots

ActionWhat it keeps
Save · ⌘SDevelopment settings in an XMP sidecar beside the source. The original image is unchanged.
Export · ⇧⌘EA rendered image for sharing or another app. Exporting is separate from saving your edit.
SnapshotAn alternate edit you can name and return to. Save to retain the snapshot state with the sidecar.

The snapshot system shows the saved and unsaved edit associated with the file. Use it to compare alternatives without rebuilding the settings each time.

Unsaved edits from the current folder are gathered together. Save them together when you want to keep the work. Choose Ignore when prompted if you intentionally want to discard pending changes—for example, after exporting a temporary variation.

Choose the right export

JPEG or HEIF with a gain map keeps an SDR rendition plus HDR information for compatible viewers. PQ HDR HEIF stores a direct HDR rendition. Choose SDR for a predictable SDR-only result. HDR appearance depends on the receiving app and display, and some sharing services remove HDR information.

08 / Work as a collection

One set of photos. One consistent look.

Lock Film captures selected settings and applies them across the photos you open and export. It is useful when you want a set to feel as though it came from one roll of film.

  1. Save or discard pending edits first. This prevents the locked settings from silently replacing unfinished work.
  2. Build your look on one photo, click the toolbar lock, and choose which settings to carry across. The Film selection includes white balance; keeping it fixed can give a set a more consistent palette.
  3. Open other photos or create a Batch Export. Locked settings also apply to export jobs, including photos you have not opened individually.
  4. After exporting, unlock to stop applying the settings. Save the resulting edits if you want to keep them, or discard the unsaved changes to keep your previous saved edits.

Unlocking stops future application of the locked settings; it does not itself undo the edits already applied. Export jobs capture their settings when created.

09 / More than RAW

Start from an SDR or HDR image, too.

You can use Dark Melon to expand an SDR image into an HDR rendition or to develop a supported HDR photo, such as an iPhone HDR image or a PQ HEIF file.

An existing HDR file can contain useful brightness information beyond SDR white, but it may already include the camera’s tone mapping and color processing. Treat it as a rendered starting point, not as untouched RAW sensor data. Expanding an SDR image cannot restore highlights that were clipped in the original.
